title: Counting the New Generation
overview: Nearly forty years after the first count at Sinai, Israel counts its fighting men again on the edge of the promised land, and of the men counted the first time, only Caleb and Joshua are left.

parts.label: A second count ordered (vv. 1-4)
parts.note: Right after the deadly plague of chapter 25, God tells Moses and Eleazar, Aaron's son and now high priest, to count every man twenty or older who could fight. Coming nearly forty years after the first count in chapter 1, this one also prepares for dividing the land among the tribes.

parts.label: Reuben and the rebels (vv. 5-11)
parts.note: The list pauses to recall Dathan and Abiram from Reuben's tribe, who joined Korah's revolt against Moses and Aaron in chapter 16 and were swallowed by the earth as a warning. Korah's own descendants survived, and their line later produced the temple singers named in several psalms.

parts.label: Tribe by tribe (vv. 12-50)
parts.note: Each tribe is listed by clans named after Jacob's grandsons and later descendants, which is how families traced who they belonged to. The brief mention of Zelophehad's five daughters (v. 33) sets up the next chapter, where they ask for a share of land because they have no brothers.

parts.label: Gains and losses (v. 51)
parts.note: The total is only about 1,800 lower than the first count, but some tribes grew while others shrank, and Simeon fell from 59,300 to 22,200. Some suggest Simeon was hit hardest by the Peor plague because Zimri, a leader of one Simeonite family, was at the center of it, but that is a guess.

parts.label: How the land will be shared (vv. 52-56)
parts.note: Larger tribes are to get more land, and the land is also to be divided by lot, a way of drawing a choice that was seen as leaving the outcome to God. The text does not explain how size and lot worked together; one old suggestion is that the lot chose the location and size set the amount, but that is an interpretation.

parts.label: Levites and a lost generation (vv. 57-65)
parts.note: The Levites, who served at the place of worship, are counted separately because they would receive no tribal land, and the list recalls Aaron's two sons who died offering fire God had not asked for. None of the men counted at Sinai remain except Caleb and Joshua, as God had said after the people refused to enter the land in chapter 14.

disagreement: Readers differ on whether the very large totals are literal headcounts or whether the Hebrew word read as 'thousand' sometimes meant a clan or military unit, which would make the numbers far smaller.
think: When one generation's choices shape what the next one inherits, how much of that weight do you think the next generation should carry?
